scope: grade 6 settled items -- widen the evidence

g6-2023-018.stem: An expression is shown below. What is the coefficient of the variable in this expression?

existingEvidence.quote: using mathematical vocabulary related to expressions, such as “coefficient,” “variable,” and “exponent.”

g6-2023-018.why: The item shows 5z + (9 ÷ 3) and asks which number is the coefficient of the variable, with 9 and 3 from the second term as distractors — pure 6.EE.2b vocabulary about the parts of an expression. This activity is the only one in grade 6 whose own text says students use the word “coefficient” about an expression, and the work itself — telling 3^x apart from 3x — is exactly the business of deciding what role a number plays in an expression. The losing reading, Unit 6 Lesson 2 “Truth and Equations,” is genuinely where 3 ⋅ x is first written as 3x, so it owns the notation; it is second best because its Warm-up asks only “What do you notice? What do you wonder?” and never names a coefficient. Recorded honestly: no grade 6 ACTIVITY asks a student to name the coefficient of an expression. The only prompt in the whole course that asks the item's question is a practice problem, Unit 6 Lesson 6 “Percentages and Equations” Problem 5b (p87), “What is the coefficient of the variable?” for 2n = 7; and the only student-facing use of the word inside an activity is Unit 6 Lesson 17's Cool-down “Interpret the Point” (p230), which hands the student the coefficient and asks what it means.

g6-2023-035.stem: Which expression is equivalent to 4(3m + 1)?

existingEvidence.quote: Select all the expressions that represent the large rectangle’s total area.

g6-2023-035.why: The item asks which expression is equivalent to 4(3m + 1), i.e. distribute a number over a sum containing a variable, with distractors that add instead of multiplying (7m + 1) or distribute to only one term (12m + 1). This Cool-down is where the curriculum tests that move: students must accept 5(b + 3), 5b + 15 and 15 + 5b as the same area and reject 3(5 + b) and 3 ⋅ 5 + 3b — the same select-the-equivalent-expression question. The losing reading, Unit 6 Lesson 11 “The Distributive Property, Part 3,” has the item's literal surface form (its table contains 3(2x + 1)) and is the only place the inner coefficient step 4 ⋅ 3m is rehearsed, but that lesson is marked optional in the pacing table, so an assessed activity in a required lesson beats an exact numeral match a class may never have seen. Medium confidence because of that missing inner-coefficient step.

g6-2023-039.stem: A set of shapes is shown below. What is the ratio of the number of circles to the total number of shapes?
figures: Two circles come first, then two squares, then one triangle -- five shapes in all.

existingEvidence.quote: Write two sentences that describe a ratio of types of animals

g6-2023-039.why: The item shows five shapes — two circles, two squares, one triangle — and asks for the ratio of circles to the total number of shapes, so the work is: read a pictured collection, count a category, count the whole, state a ratio. This Cool-down is the assessed version of exactly that: a pictured collection of dogs, mice and cats with the instruction to write ratio sentences about it. The losing reading, Unit 2 Lesson 15 “Part-Part-Whole Ratios” (Cubes of Paint, p223), is where the parts of a ratio are first related to their total (5 ml red and 3 ml blue make 8 ml maroon), which is the one idea this Cool-down lacks; it is second best because its own question is “how many millilitres of maroon paint will there be,” a total, never a part-to-whole ratio. Worth recording: grade 6 asks for part-to-part ratios only — no activity in the course asks a student to write a part-to-total ratio, so the item's exact form is unrehearsed either way.

g6-2023-044.stem: The tables below show the ratios of distance to time traveled by Car A and Car B. If both cars maintain their rates of speed, what is the difference between the distances, in miles, traveled by Car A and by Car B after 8 hours?
figures: Car A: 2 hours 130 miles, 4 hours 260, 6 hours 390. Car B: 3 hours 186 miles, 5 hours 310, 7 hours 434.

existingEvidence.quote: They both walk for 30 seconds. At these rates, how far apart

g6-2023-044.why: The item gives two distance-time tables (Car A 65 mph, Car B 62 mph), extends both to 8 hours and asks for the difference in distance. This Cool-down is the only place in grade 6 that poses that whole question: two movers at constant rates given as ratios, a shared elapsed time, and how far apart they end up. The losing reading, Unit 3 Lesson 6 “Equivalent Ratios Have the Same Unit Rates” (Cheetah Speed, p110), is the non-optional runner-up and does the item's heavy lifting — a time/distance/speed table with a distance to be found for a time that is not listed — but it never asks for a comparison, and its table hands students a speed column that the item's tables do not. Lesson 9 is marked optional in the pacing table, so this evidence is weaker than its fit suggests; a class that skipped it has met the difference question only in the Unit 2 Lesson 14 Warm-up (p205), “A red car and a blue car ... How far apart are they after 4 hours?”, which withholds the rates on purpose.

figures: They differ in whether the circle at negative 3 is filled or open and in whether the shaded ray runs left or right.

existingEvidence.quote: closed (include) or open (exclude) circle at the boundary of the constraint

g6-2024-011.why: The item shows four number lines and asks which represents x ≥ −3; they differ only in whether the circle at −3 is filled and which way the ray is shaded, so the item is a match-a-math-statement-to-a-graph task turning on the endpoint convention. This card sort is precisely that — stories, descriptions of values, math statements and number lines matched to each other — and it is where the curriculum makes the closed-versus-open circle decision explicit. The losing reading, Unit 7 Lesson 9 “Solutions of Inequalities,” asks students to draw a number line for w < 1; it is second best because it runs in the opposite direction (draw, not choose) and its inequality is strict, so the closed circle that decides this item is never exercised there.

g6-2024-015.stem: Ben purchases 1 14 pounds of nuts and puts them into bags. Each bag holds 18 pound of nuts. He uses all the nuts to fill each bag completely. How many bags does Ben fill with nuts?
g6-2024-015.why: The item puts 1 1/4 pounds of nuts into 1/8-pound bags and asks how many bags. This Warm-up asks “How many 1/8 s are in 1 1/4 ?” — the item's exact numbers, exact question and exact answer of 10 — in a required lesson, and its distractor 5/32 is what multiplying instead of dividing produces. The losing reading, Unit 4 Lesson 6 “Using Diagrams to Find the Number of Groups” (Finding the Number of Groups, p95), asks the same question in the item's own units (“How many groups of 1/2 pound are in 2 3/4 pounds?”) and is the contextual version of the task; it is second best only because the numbers and phrasing of this item appear verbatim one lesson earlier.

g6-2024-031.stem: There are 104 calories in an 8-ounce serving of soda. How many calories are in 1 ounce of soda?

existingEvidence.quote: How many gallons of detergent does the laundry service use per week?

g6-2024-031.why: The item gives 104 calories in an 8-ounce serving and asks for the calories in 1 ounce, so the per-1 value is itself the answer, in a context that is not a price. This activity is where the term unit rate is introduced as the amount of one quantity per 1 of the other, and its first question — 10 gallons of detergent every 6 weeks, how many gallons per week — is the item's division in a non-price setting. The losing reading, Unit 2 Lesson 8 “How Much for One?”, is where the per-1 move is first taught and is a fair second best, but every one of its tasks is a unit PRICE (cost per bottle, per bag, per book); the generalisation to any pair of quantities, which is what this item needs, happens here in Unit 3.

g6-2024-036.stem: A tutoring company charges $25.00 per hour to tutor a student. How many hours o f tutoring would cost $62.50 ?

existingEvidence.quote: Each notebook costs 5.70. How many notebooks does Diego buy

g6-2024-036.why: The item gives a rate ($25.00 per hour) and a total ($62.50) and asks for the number of hours, so a student must set up 25x = 62.50 and solve it, landing on a non-whole-number answer. The second reading's lesson stands — Unit 6 Lesson 5 is where a situation is matched to an equation and then solved — but the tighter evidence inside it is this Cool-down rather than Activity 2: its second question is the item with different nouns, a unit price and a total with the three candidate equations x + 5.7 = 17.1, 5.7x = 17.1 and 17.1x = 5.7. The losing reading, Unit 6 Lesson 4 “Practice Solving Equations” (Row Game, p61), does contain px = q equations with non-whole solutions such as 6x = 45; it is second best because it supplies the equation ready-made and the item's real demand is building it from the situation.

g6-2024-037.stem: The four vertices of a parallelogram are plotted on the coordinate plane shown below. What is the distance, in units, between vertices A and D ?
figures: A is at negative 6, 6; D is at 4, 6; B is at 2, negative 4; C is at 12, negative 4.

existingEvidence.quote: What is the distance between points C and D?

g6-2024-037.why: The item supplies a plotted parallelogram and asks the distance between A(−6, 6) and D(4, 6) — one horizontal length read off a grid that is already drawn. This Cool-down asks the item's question word for word, of points already plotted. The losing reading, Unit 7 Lesson 15 “Shapes in the Coordinate Plane” (Perimeter of a Polygon, p187), is the lesson the curriculum itself tags with NY-6.G.3 and it does compute side lengths from coordinates; it is second best because it asks for a perimeter and makes students plot the figure from a list of vertices first, and this item hands the figure over and asks for a single distance.

g6-2024-042.stem: Mike needs a ticket every time he rides the bus. Given the equation c = 2.75t, what is the relationship between t, the number of tickets that Mike buys, and c, the total cost? Be sure to identify which variable is independent and which variable is dependent in your answer.

placement.lessonTitle: Tables, Equations, and Graphs, Oh My!

existingEvidence.quote: How the dependent variable and independent variable are related.

g6-2024-042.why: The item hands the student the equation c = 2.75t and asks two things: describe the relationship in words, and say which variable is independent and which is dependent. That is this activity's stated deliverable — students must be prepared to explain what each variable represents and how the dependent and independent variables are related — for an equation they were given, several of which (E = 6s, m = 8.96V, g = 28.35z) have exactly this item's rate-times-a-variable form. The losing reading, Unit 6 Lesson 16 “Two Related Quantities, Part 1,” is where the two terms are coined, and that is a real claim; it is second best because Lesson 16's work runs situation-to-equation (build a table, then write the equation) while this item runs equation-to-description, which is what Lesson 19 is built to do.

g6-2025-035.stem: Hannah buys oranges and apples from the grocery store. She pays $6.25 for 5 pounds of oranges and $6.90 for 6 pounds of apples. Which statement about the fruit is true?
choices: Apples have the greater unit price at $1.15.
Apples have the greater unit price at $1.25.
Oranges have the greater unit price at $1.15.
Oranges have the greater unit price at $1.25.

existingEvidence.quote: students compare rates per 1 in a shopping context

g6-2025-035.why: The item gives $6.25 for 5 pounds of oranges and $6.90 for 6 pounds of apples and asks which statement about the two unit prices is true, so both prices per 1 must be computed ($1.25 and $1.15) and compared. This activity is the curriculum's shopping comparison of prices per 1, with each price given as “n for $X” exactly as the item gives them. The losing reading, Unit 3 Lesson 5 “Interpreting Rates” (Laundry Detergent and Raffle Tickets, p89), is where unit rates are named and computed and would produce both of the item's numbers; it is second best because it never compares the two situations it sets up, and comparison is the item's actual question. Medium confidence: this activity, and the Cool-down “Sparkling Water” in the same lesson, ask which price is LOWER, while the item asks which is greater.

g6-2025-041.stem: A restaurant buys cheese in large blocks. The table below shows the relationship between the number of blocks of cheese, b, that they buy, and the total amount paid, t, in dollars. Based on the data in the table, write an equation to represent the total price, t, in terms of the number of blocks of cheese bought, b. Be sure to identify the independent and dependent variables in your explanation.
figures: 2 blocks for 112 dollars, 4 for 224, 6 for 336, and 8 for 448.

existingEvidence.quote: allows students to interpret and write equations with variables

g6-2025-041.why: The item gives a table of cheese blocks against dollars paid and asks for an equation for t in terms of b, plus which variable is independent and which dependent. This activity runs in that direction: students complete a table of equivalent ratios, describe how one quantity relates to the other, write equations with two variables from it, and the Activity Synthesis is where “dependent variable” and “independent variable” are introduced. The losing reading, Unit 6 Lesson 19 “Tables, Equations, and Graphs, Oh My!” (Card Sort: Equations and Tables, p249), does pair tables with equations, but every equation there is handed to the student ready-made — Lesson 19 never has anyone write one from a table, which is the item's whole demand. Medium because the only task in the course that literally asks for an equation written from a table is the Cool-down of Lesson 18 (p243), and Lesson 18 is optional.

g6-2026-006.stem: Which expression represents the perimeter, in units, of the figure shown below?
figures: Going round the figure the sides are 2, x, 5, 2, x plus 3, and 6.

existingEvidence.activity: Partitioned Rectangles When Lengths Are Unknown
existingEvidence.quote: Write an expression for the sum of the areas of the two rectangles.

g6-2026-006.why: The item adds the six labelled sides of an L-shaped figure (2, x, 5, 2, x + 3, 6) into 2x + 18, so it wants an expression for a figure's total measurement built from parts, two of which carry a variable, with the x terms and the constants each collected. The gap the first reading reported is real and I verified it: NO grade 6 activity anywhere asks for a perimeter expression containing a variable. “Perimeter” appears in only three student tasks in the whole course — a units Warm-up (U1 L16), the Cool-down of the OPTIONAL Unit 6 Lesson 18 (a P-and-side-length table, p243), and a numeric polygon perimeter from coordinates (U7 L15) — and the one variable perimeter in grade 6 is a practice problem in the OPTIONAL Unit 6 Lesson 11 (p148, “the perimeter of a square with side length s cm”). So this is the closest available, not a true match: here students write an expression for a figure's total measurement when one length is unknown, producing the item's constant-plus-variable-term shape (40 + 5x), in a required lesson of the unit that owns NY-6.EE.6. The losing reading, Unit 1 Lesson 18 “Surface Area of a Cube” (Every Cube in the Whole World, p305), does build a total measurement from a variable edge length; it is second best because all six of its parts are identical, so it produces 6s² with no constant term and none of the like-term collection across unlike lengths that decides this item's distractors.

g6-2026-014.stem: A pizza shop charges $15.00 for each large pizza. There is a one time charge of $5.00 to deliver any number of pizzas. Which equation could be used to determine the total charge, c, in dollars, of a delivery order of p large pizzas?

existingEvidence.quote: Select all equations that can represent the relationship between b

g6-2026-014.why: The item describes a situation — $15 per large pizza plus a one-time $5 delivery charge — and asks which equation could be used for the total charge c of p pizzas, with distractors (c = 15 + 5p, c = 15 × 5 + p) that turn on which quantity carries the multiplier. This Cool-down is the curriculum's test of that exact choice: given a relationship between two quantities, select all the equations that can represent it, from a list (w = 1/2 b, b = 1/2 w, b = w, b = 2w, w = 2b) whose whole point is which variable takes the coefficient. The losing reading, Unit 6 Lesson 19 “Tables, Equations, and Graphs, Oh My!” (Getting to Know an Equation, p250), runs the other way — it hands out equations and asks what situation they describe — so it is second best for an item that starts from a situation. Medium, and both readings were right to flag it: no grade 6 activity writes a two-variable equation that combines a rate with a fixed amount; every relationship in Unit 6 Section D is a single operation, so the +5 in this item is unrehearsed.

g6-2026-021.stem: Tina makes 6 paper decorations in 39 minutes. At this rate, how many minutes will it take Tina to make 14 paper decorations?

placement.lessonTitle: Navigating a Table of Equivalent Ratios

existingEvidence.quote: At this rate, how much would Lin be paid for 3 hours of work?

g6-2026-021.why: The item gives 6 decorations in 39 minutes and asks about 14 decorations, where 14 is not a multiple of 6, so the way through is the per-1 value (6.5 minutes each) used as an intermediate step to a scaled answer of 91 minutes. This activity exists for that difficulty: $90 for 5 hours, then 8 hours, 3 hours and 2.1 hours, with the narrative naming the two insights — that corresponding quantities are not always multiples of each other, and that an equivalent ratio with a value of 1 is the helpful middle step. The losing reading, Unit 3 Lesson 8 “Solving Rate Problems” (Window Washing, p132), is also built on a non-multiple target and is a genuine second best; it loses because its 24,348 windows make it a modelling task about choosing a strategy at scale, while this item is the small, clean scale-through-1 that Lesson 12 introduces.

g6-2026-031.stem: A teacher surveyed all of the students in the art club to determine their favorite ice cream flavor. Each student chose one flavor. The results of the survey are shown in the table below. What percent of the students in the art club chose vanilla ice cream as their favorite flavor?

existingEvidence.quote: students determine what percentage one number is of another number

g6-2026-031.why: The item gives an art-club survey table (chocolate 18, vanilla 21, strawberry 11) and asks what percent chose vanilla, so students must total the table to 50 and then answer “21 is what percentage of 50?” This Warm-up asks that question form directly and its pairs are related by benchmark factors, which is exactly what 50 to 100 is — double it and 21 becomes 42. It is in a required lesson. The losing reading, Unit 3 Lesson 16 “Finding the Percentage” (Restaurant Capacity, p250), is the closer numerical analogue and its own Cool-down even uses a school of 50 people; it is second best because the pacing table marks the whole of Lesson 16 optional, so a class may never have met it. Medium: no percentage activity in grade 6 makes students build the whole by summing a table first, which is the step this item adds.

g6-2026-034.stem: A store has a sale on one type of notebook. The price of 3 of these notebooks is $6. Which table shows the same relationship for each given number of notebooks of this type and the total price for those notebooks?
figures: Each pairs a number of notebooks with a price in dollars. They differ in which row holds which values and in whether the prices double the notebook counts or the other way round.

placement.lessonTitle: Tables and Double Number Line Diagrams

existingEvidence.quote: Do you agree that this table represents the situation?

g6-2026-034.why: The item says 3 notebooks cost $6 and asks which of four tables shows that relationship; the distractors swap which row holds the counts and which the prices, or scale the wrong quantity. This Warm-up asks the item's question outright — it hands students a headerless table that conflicts with the situation described (3,000 sitting in the wrong place) and asks whether it really represents it — so both of the item's failure modes, wrong placement and wrong scaling, are what students must check. The losing reading, Unit 3 Lesson 6 “Equivalent Ratios Have the Same Unit Rates” (Binders and Notebooks, p100), supplies the test each candidate table must pass, that every row shares one unit rate, and even uses notebooks and prices; it is second best because students there complete a table they are told is correct rather than judging whether a table represents a situation at all.

g6-2026-044.stem: Two stores sell the same size rolls of paper towels in different packages. • Store A sells 6 rolls for $12.24 • Store B sells 9 rolls for $19.62 Which store has the lower price per roll of paper towels? Be sure to include the unit rate for each store in your answer.

existingEvidence.quote: A store sells wooden rulers in packs of 10 and packs of 6.

g6-2026-044.why: The item gives Store A at 6 rolls for $12.24 and Store B at 9 rolls for $19.62, asks which has the lower price per roll, and requires the unit rate for each store in the answer. This Cool-down is the same task with equally unfriendly money: two pack sizes of one product ($8.49 for 10, $5.40 for 6), compute both prices per one, say which is better and explain how you know. The losing reading, Unit 3 Lesson 4 “Comparing Speeds and Prices” (The Best Deal on Beans, p77), is where comparing prices per 1 while shopping is introduced and is a fair second best; it loses because it spreads the comparison over four ads and asks only for the winner, where this Cool-down is the assessed two-offer version the item copies.
